en: Preface to the Words of Chan Master Lin Holding the Whisk:
When my late master reached the age of eighty, he knew in advance that the time for his nirvana had arrived.

He then transmitted the Great Dharma to Chan Master Master Lin and commanded him to lead the assembly in holding the whisk. Upon hearing his exhortations, the assembly was greatly pleased and submitted with deep respect. Not long after, the old man manifested...
After his passing, the eminent master Zhongqiang succeeded him, and the Great Wheel of Dharma turned as if the Elder were still hale and hearty.

At that time, the brothers of this same school deliberated together and requested that the Master take up the whisk to deliver his discourse, which was subsequently carved into woodblocks for circulation. They further entreated me to compose a preface for the beginning of the volumes.
I consider the Chan Master’s appearance in the world to be like the rising sun in the east, its light piercing through the entire universe.
Who among those with eyes would not see this? Furthermore, what need is there for a preface? Nevertheless, having received the request of the assembly, I have not declined to set down these weeds;
I merely record the origins of the matter. Thus ends the title, followed by the respectful salutation of the Dharma-brother Chuanshanhe.
Four Instances of Holding the Whisk; Three Instances of Tea Discourses; Six Instances of Citing Ancient Precedents;
Twelve Instances of Buddhist Rituals; Twenty-Eight Verses; Seventeen Odes; Twenty-Two Eulogies;
and Seven Articles of Mournful Petition for Gulin (attached).
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Weilin of Gushan, while serving as Head Seat and Holding the Whisk,
Volume One.
Compiled by Taijing.
On the day of the Dharma-transmission ceremony, the Old Master (the Abbot) commanded [the Master] to hold the whisk. The Master said: "Before the Multi-Child Stupa is the seamless robe;
within the room of Huangmei is the tattered cassock. Today my teacher personally transmits it to me; the iron tree once again blooms with five petals.
Is there anyone here who can provide mutual testimony? A monk asked: "Having received the direct instruction and established the Dharma and the Sangha, when the great assembly ascends..."

[The monk] came specifically to offer congratulations. The Master said, "What is there to congratulate? The monk replied, "Auspicious colors bloom atop Shigufeng Peak; auspicious clouds span ten thousand *li*, encompassing the entire universe.

The Master said, "I leave it to you to offer such praise. The monk replied, "Clearly I raise this up to inform all quarters: the waters of Dong Creek flow upstream, surging in waves ten thousand feet high. The Master said, "Be careful not to transmit false news. A monk asked: [The Master said: "What is there to congratulate? [The monk] replied: "Auspicious colors bloom atop Shigufeng Peak; auspicious clouds span ten thousand *li*, encompassing the entire universe.

The Master said: "I leave it to you to offer such praise. [The monk] replied: "Clearly I raise this up to inform all quarters: the waters of Dong Creek flow upstream, surging in waves ten thousand feet high. The Master said: "Be careful not to transmit false news. A monk asked:

The stone drums resound through the void; the great earth leans its ears. Setting aside for a moment the question of the "crescent moon" and the "long serpent," how is it that the son inherits his father’s legacy?
The Master spreads both hands. Jin says, “Truly, a golden-haired lion emerges from its cave; its roar shakes heaven and earth, and all other species are startled.
The Master says, “It is no hindrance to bear witness. Jin says, “The jade hooves trample the moon upon the clear pool; the golden horns prop up—”
"Opening the sky beyond the clouds: when the Great Function manifests before one, how can it be established? The Master then gave a shout.
The monk stepped forward and said, "The Head Seat in the hall is naturally free and at ease. The Master said, "After you have prostrated, withdraw.
A monk asked, "All speech belongs to the category of turbid phrases; I ask from within a turbid phrase, so please answer me with a pure phrase. The Master said, "Your back!"
"What is it after this? The monk bowed and said, "I thank the Master for his answer. The Master did not respond. The monk asked, "The spring breeze is vast and sweeping, auspicious vapors swirl;
as a Dharma heir of the Dharma King, you continue the ancestral wind. Before the assembly of humans and devas today, I wonder what it is that you transmit? The Master held up his whisk.
The monk stepped forward and said, "The one phrase of direct presence has been pointed out by the Master; [it is] the Cavern..."
"What is the matter regarding the supreme vehicle? The Master said, "A lacquer bucket emits light. The monk bowed.
The monk asked, "In the past, when Qingfeng answered the question of Head Administrator Ze with 'The boy Bingding comes seeking fire,' Ze did not awaken.
Fayan also answered with 'The boy Bingding comes seeking fire,' yet he awakened. I do not know how it was that he attained awakening."
[The Master] spoke of this principle. The Master said, "Today you have questioned me. [The student] stepped forward and said, "The night is still and the water cold; the fish do not take the bait.
The boat returns empty under the bright moon. The Master said, "Idle words. Is there anyone else who would like to ask a question? The assembly remained silent.
The Master then said: "To cite the ancients and cite the present is like bringing forth leftover soup and rancid rice; there is no need to do so.

Try to utter a single word from within your own breast—how regrettable that your tongue is too short! To point directly in the presence of all, you have already delayed by eight hours. As for the path before sound—"
Be careful not to speak of it. Therefore, throughout the three periods of time, the Buddhas have had no door through which to enter this matter;

even the entire Great Canon of Teachings cannot adequately explain or manifest it. Even if Yunmen, Caodong, Linji, or Deshan were to arrive here, they would have nothing for it but to fold their hands in surrender, left staring blankly behind.
Suddenly, if there were a man who, upon hearing such words, were to immediately cease his mental activity—*xiexqixin*.
The monkey stilled the mind-horse; at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, he let go and cast off his body, causing the root of life to be suddenly severed and all breath to cease.
Only then did he revive and arise, leaping and bounding within the void.
He took a single blade of grass and used it as a sixteen-foot golden body; he took the sixteen-foot golden body and used it as a single blade of grass, stirring the long...
The rivers shall become butter and curd; the great earth shall be transformed into gold.

For the people of the world, he will have ample leisure to untangle their entanglements, remove their bonds, relieve their hunger, and succor their poverty. Is there anyone who can truly fulfill the original vow of leaving home and traveling on pilgrimage?
If there is, the Buddha-dharma has someone to rely upon. If this is not yet the case, I cannot help but pour a second ladle of foul water over you.
He then raised his whisk and called to the assembly, saying, "Is this not right here? Do you not see it?
He struck the desk once and said, "Do you not hear it? Since you both see and hear it, what exactly is it?
*Dot!* What else could it be? He spoke again, saying, "Dàohuì has the honor of sitting beneath the old Master's seat."
For over ten years, I have received the most exhaustive care and nurturing from the frost and snow; yet, alas, my nature is so dull and sluggish that I have accomplished nothing at all.
Today, I humbly receive your compassionate decree, entrusting me with the robe and whisk before this assembly of devas and humans to uphold and transmit them.
Furthermore, you command me to occupy the First Seat and wield the whisk to preach the Dharma for my fellow brothers, as if conferring upon me the precious throne itself.
To receive this instruction directly upon my ordinary and mediocre self fills me with nothing but shame and trepidation. Nevertheless, grievances have their origins and debts have their owners;
having arrived at this point, there can be no further evasion. I can do nothing but venture to accept it.

Furthermore, the brothers present here are all long-standing practitioners from the late Master’s assembly—eminent scholars and renowned masters who have humbled themselves to join this lowly gathering and participate together in the Dharma feast. Thus, we shall proceed.
I am deeply moved and profoundly grateful for this influence. Furthermore, I cite a verse by the founding patriarch, National Teacher Yan, which says:

"Directly beneath, it is still difficult to comprehend; Seeking through words only makes it more remote. If one discusses Buddhas and Patriarchs, They are, quite simply, separated by the ends of the earth.

The National Teacher raised this question to a monk, saying, "How do you understand this? The monk was speechless. Thereupon, the National Teacher said to his attendant, "Please explain this for him..."
"Someone provides a substitute phrase on behalf of another. The monk said, "When the Master speaks thus, he has already been separated from the edge of the world by ten thousand *li*.
The monk reported this to the National Teacher. The National Teacher called his attendant and asked, "Did you provide that phrase for this monk? The attendant replied, "I did."
The National Teacher beat him and drove him out of the monastery. The Master said, "Although the National Teacher has issued his command, how can it be that the attendant's words still remain?

Nevertheless, 'the official may not admit even a needle, yet private matters allow for carriages and horses. Today, Upāsaka Dai continues the 'dog's tail' following the 'fox fur,' and he too has a verse.
I cannot help but present it to the assembly. He then said: "Upa Daren, Qiu Yiji, Hua..."

[He remained silent for] three thousand [moments]. After a long while, he smiled and said, "One may know the propriety of ritual. He continued, "I humbly entreat the great assembly to stand for a long time;

take care of yourselves. Holding the whisk, he said: "Today, the Abbot’s Ninth Brother, the Prior, because the Old Monk has not ascended the hall for a long time, requested that I, the Venerable Pai, speak a few words of the Buddha-Dharma to create karmic conditions with the assembly.
As for these two characters, 'Buddha-Dharma,' they are truly not easy to discuss."

Even to hear it being spoken is not easy. If one hears it as it truly is—even a single verse or half a verse—and stores it within the field of the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*), it will forever serve as the seed for the Path throughout every world and every lifetime. How much more so if one can believe, understand, practice, and realize it!
Now, let us take one verse from among the scriptures and deliberate upon it together with the assembly. As it says in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
A single hair manifests spiritual transformations; all Buddhas speak of it together. Even after passing through immeasurable kalpas, one cannot reach its limit.

I venture to ask the great assembly: the dimension of a single hair is extremely minute, the wisdom and eloquence of all Buddhas are exceedingly vast, and the duration of immeasurable kalpas is exceedingly long. Why, then, can its limit not be reached? You must know that this single hair is high.
It has no summit; it is deep without bottom; it is lateral without boundary; it is central without location.

Yet, it does not destroy the appearance of a single hair. Throughout the entire universe and great earth, the myriad phenomena of the forest—whether sentient or insentient—all emerge and subside within this single hair.
Furthermore, there is no measure of such emergence or subsidence; each is unaware of the other. Each is...
They meet. If one hair is thus, all hairs are likewise; that is to say, so it is with every atom, so it is with every dharma, so it is with every thought-moment.

Is there anyone who can discern and clarify this? If one can discern and clarify it, then all Buddhas, with one voice and many mouths, would proclaim that the spiritual transformations manifested by this single hair could not reach their limit even after passing through immeasurable kalpas. This is the principle.
It is so. This is not beyond one's capacity. Should this not yet be the case, you should first investigate it within this single hair.
If you can thoroughly penetrate this single hair through diligent study, then there will be no need to laboriously travel to a hundred cities to consult various masters;
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates will be realized all at once. Have you not seen how Master Shaolao asked?
Mazu was asked, "What is the great meaning of the West? Mazu said, "Pay your respects. Just as Shuilao was about to prostrate, Mazu stepped on him and knocked him down.

Shuilao attained great enlightenment; rising up, he clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "A hundred thousand samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings are all contained within the tip of a single hair.
Once you recognize the source, you have gone beyond. Later, [he spoke again].
He spoke self-deprecatingly: "Ever since I was kicked by Master Ma, I have laughed without ceasing until this very day.
But tell me, what exactly is it that he laughs at, incessantly? *Du!* A beggar sees only small profit. Take care!"
The Old Monk, upon celebrating his eightieth birthday, opened the Great Canon of the Tripitaka and held the whisk. A monk asked, "I do not ask about the entire Great Canon of Teachings;
what is it like when both person and dharma are forgotten? The Master remained silent for a long while.

The monk pressed further, "Is there any other way to communicate this message? The Master said, "Greatly insatiable. The monk continued, "When the sea dries up and its bottom is revealed, only then does the dragon appear. When the moon sets..."

The waves submerge their traces in the heart of the water. The Master said, "Idle talk. A monk asked, "The World-Honored One preached the Dharma for forty-nine years and delivered over three hundred assemblies of sutras.
Yet at the end, he held up a flower to show the assembly, which is called the 'Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings.
What is this one phrase of the Separate Transmission? The Master held up his whisk. The monk said, "Thank you for the instruction, Master. The Master said, "Clever."
A monk asked, "Within the teachings and beyond the teachings, all are but verbose words. Without involving any literary artifice, please let me borrow a glimpse.

The Master said, "You have already added one more question to this. The monk gave a shout and said, "Look at this fellow; today he has suffered a total defeat! The Master said, "Go out and take it upon yourself.
He then continued, "In years past, the layman Huang Zhi-san once provided funds for the printing of [this work] for our own mountain monastery."
The Great Canon has been produced. On the nineteenth day of the seventh month this year, we humbly encounter the eightieth anniversary of the Venerable Master’s birth.
Two disciples from the neighboring counties have specially invited the assembly of monks to open this Great Canon, offering prayers for the Venerable Master’s longevity.
We dedicate these merits to praying for the prosperity of the state and planting blessings for the people. Just as it is said: [The text continues with the formal dedication.]

Within the Great Canon there are over seven thousand scrolls—sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and the writings of the masters of the three schools—so numerous as to exceed the capacity of oxen to carry or rafters to hold.
Yet tell me: is there even a single character among them that is fundamental?
Old Monk, you who conceal yourself beyond the kalpas and guide beings in accordance with the times—how can one offer a blessing for your longevity? If you can respond here...
If you attain even one eye, you will know that before Śākyamuni the Old Man had opened his mouth, he had already finished opening the treasury;

and before the Old Monk had yet been born, he had already finished bestowing blessings for longevity. If this is not yet the case, we cannot help but set up a tangle of complications and bind empty space upside down.
He then took up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have only spoken..."
This very thing was taught by Śākyamuni Buddha; this very thing is also taught today by Elder Huì.
But tell me, how is this thing to be explained? He strikes the ground once and says: "This is the Sūtra-piṭaka. Again he strikes once and says:
"This is the Vinaya-piṭaka. Once more he strikes once and says: "This is the Abhidharma-piṭaka. It possesses the provisional and the real; it possesses the sudden."

There is gradualness; there are phenomena, principles, causes, and effects. The three stages of worthiness, the ten stages of sagehood, and the four paths and four fruits each practice and realize according to their respective capacities.
Yet this very thing is neither provisional nor real, neither sudden nor gradual;

it is neither phenomenon nor principle, neither cause nor effect. It is not the three stages of worthiness, nor the ten stages of sagehood; it does not belong to cultivation, nor does it belong to realization. Great assembly!
This entire Great Canon has already been beheld directly before one’s very eyes. But tell me, how should it be read? Long ago, Master Lumen said:
"The entire earth is a single volume of scripture for the student. He also said: "The entire universe is the single eye of the śramaṇa.
With such an eye, look upon such a scripture; thus, for ten million billion kalpas, there shall be no interruption.
The Old Man Wansong said: "To read and study this is no easy task. Even if you were to do so, you would only manage to read half of the Tripitaka;
to hope to master this entire Great Canon is still a very long way off. But as for this Great Canon, how exactly are you to read and study it?
After a long silence, he said: "A single snap of the fingers completes the eighty thousand gates; in an instant, the three great kalpas are extinguished. Furthermore...
[The Master] struck the desk three times, gave a shout, and then raised the following case: A monk asked Shoushan, "Master Chan Master, how old are you?
Shoushan said, "I am of the same age as empty space. The monk said, "How old is empty space? Shoushan said, "It is of the same age as this old monk.
The Master said: "He existed before heaven and earth but was not born; he exists after heaven and earth but does not grow old. Without past, there is no present."
Neither extended nor shortened—this is the life-span of Mount Shou. If someone were to ask the Old Monk today how many years he has lived, simply tell them:
"The peaks soar to heaven, a thousand ages of splendor; the spiritual source penetrates the sea, ten thousand years of clarity."
Now tell me, how far apart are you from the ancients? If you can discern this here, you may come personally to offer congratulations on the old monk’s birthday.
If you cannot discern it, feel free to go through the seven hundred cases of the Tripitaka from beginning to end. Take care.
On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, the precepts were conferred. The two bodhisattvas Shideng and Xinjian requested that the Master hold the whisk and deliver a general discourse.
A monk asked, "What is the 'partial within the central'? The Master said, "A pillar stands before the courtyard. The monk pressed further, "What is the 'central within the partial'?
The Master said, "What do you call a pillar? The monk asked again, "What is the 'coming from the central'? The Master then gave a shout.
The student asked, "What is 'reaching within the simultaneous'? The Master said, "For today, let me simply engage in a reversal with you.
The student asked, "What is 'arriving within the simultaneous'? The Master said, "I shall tell you tomorrow.

The student said, "If that is so, then the iron ox bellows forth beyond the vast sky, and the golden palace, layer upon layer, reveals the Most Honored One. He then bowed. The Master then said, "Since the beginningless kalpas..."
The matter lies entirely in this very moment. [He] suddenly picks up his staff and says: "Today, the Elder Śākyamuni attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment upon the tip of Pre’s staff.
Do you all see? [He] strikes the ground once with the staff and says: "Furthermore, he sighs in wonder:
'All sentient beings are fully endowed with the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it.'"
Realization. Do you all hear this? If you can hear it directly right now, there is no hindrance to realizing the same as Śākyamuni Buddha.
If you can see it directly right now, there is no hindrance to accomplishing the same as Śākyamuni Buddha. Since you realize the same and accomplish the same, [you are one with him].
At this very moment, Śākyamuni is none other than your own selves;
your own selves are none other than Śākyamuni. If your own selves are Śākyamuni, then the self cannot be apprehended.
If Śākyamuni is your own selves, then Śākyamuni likewise cannot be apprehended. Even realization cannot be apprehended.
Attainment is unattainable; accomplishment is also unattainable; deluded conceptualization and attachment are also unattainable; the marks of wisdom and virtue are also unattainable.
Even this very "unattainability" is unattainable. Now tell me, what is this? After a long silence, he said:
"The skin has fallen away entirely; there remains only the single reality. He then cast down his staff and spoke again:

"Today is the anniversary of the World-Honored One’s attainment of enlightenment. I am humbled that various mountain dharma friends, admiring the legacy of the late Senior Master, have come specifically to this mountain to seek the precepts.
Furthermore, I am honored that the two bodhisattvas Shideng and Xinjian have traveled from afar to provide a vegetarian feast."
With earnest and respectful entreaty, he requested the essential path. He then bestowed upon the assembly of precept-disciples an illumination of the principle of the precepts.
Now, the single character for "precept" (*śīla*) has the meaning of preventing wrongdoing and ceasing evil. One must know that the fundamental substance of one’s own mind is originally without "is";
where, then, is there "non-is"? It is fundamentally without "good"; where, then, can "evil" be attached? Without good or evil, without "is" or "non-is."
It is pure, starkly naked, and brilliantly clear. Yet, alas, sentient beings do not realize this in their daily lives.
Because they do not realize it, they falsely fabricate wrong within that which is beyond right and wrong; they falsely give rise to evil within that which is beyond good and evil.

Consequently, the three poisons blaze within while the six sense-objects defile them from without. Thus they are submerged within the three realms and revolve amidst the four modes of birth, lost in delusion.
In the ocean of suffering, there is no time of escape. For this reason, when the World-Honored One attained the Way, he first established the precepts and laws.

These were intended, for the time being, to prevent what is wrong and cease evil, and to restore what is right and cultivate goodness. When goodness reaches its limit, evil is transformed; when evil is transformed, even goodness no longer exists.
When the ultimate is reached, non-being is forgotten; when non-being is forgotten, even being cannot be established. It is like borrowing a path.
Upon returning home, one leaves the road once home is reached; one takes a boat to reach the shore, yet discards the boat once the shore is reached.

It is also like the weapons of a state, which are increasingly employed to quell disorder and execute the wicked for the sake of securing the realm and stabilizing the nation—used only when there is no other choice.
Nevertheless, although the precepts are numerous, they do not exceed four types: namely, the five precepts, the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, and the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu.
There are one hundred and fifty precepts, namely the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of a bodhisattva.
Although these four types of precepts differ according to whether they belong to the mundane or supramundane, or the Hīnayāna or Mahāyāna, they all take the five precepts as their foundation.
If the root is deep, the branches and leaves will naturally flourish. Regarding the five precepts: first, not killing; second, not stealing;
third, not engaging in sexual misconduct; fourth, not lying; fifth, not drinking intoxicants.

Anyone who receives the precepts must clearly understand what is to be ceased and what is to be practiced within these five precepts, and skillfully master their observance and transgression. For example, "not killing" is a precept of cessation, through which one protects all sentient beings.

To give life is "active" (kriyā); to observe the precept against killing is "retention" (dhāraṇa); to kill intentionally is "transgression. As with not stealing being "cessation" (virati), practicing the dāna-pāramitā is "active";

observing the precept against stealing is "retention"; and seeking through unrighteous greed is "transgression. As with not committing sexual misconduct being "cessation," [so it is for the other precepts].

To diligently cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya) is "action" (kriyā); to refrain from sexual misconduct is "observance" (samvara). For the arising of defiled thoughts within is a "transgression.

Just as refraining from false speech is "cessation" (virati), speaking truthfully, speaking with integrity, speaking gently, and speaking harmoniously is "action"; to refrain from lying is "observance."

Therefore, intentional drinking is an offense. For example, "not drinking alcohol" is an abstinence; "practicing the karma of wisdom" is an undertaking; "refraining from drinking" is observance; and "intentionally drinking" is an offense.
If one merely observes [the precepts] without offending, abstains [from the prohibited] without undertaking [the virtuous], this is the fivefold precept of humans and devas.

If one observes [the precepts] without offending, abstains [from the prohibited] while also undertaking [the virtuous], yet remains settled only in self-benefit and is unable to benefit others, this is the Śrāvaka.

The five precepts: if one uses these to maintain restraint and avoid transgressions for one's own benefit, and likewise uses them to extensively transform sentient beings, these are the five precepts of a bodhisattva.
There is only this single set of five precepts; it is solely due to the differences among those who uphold them that such various distinctions arise.

Furthermore, you must know that while the śrāvakas’ observance of precepts involves merely restraining the body without practicing the mind, the bodhisattva’s observance of precepts aims directly at restraining the mind so that it does not arise.
This proceeds from the shallow to the deep, and from the near to the far; it is like the method of eating sugarcane upside down, gradually entering a state of excellence.
O virtuous ones, there is no peace in the three realms and the four elements are insubstantial. Time cannot be grasped or toyed with; life...
Death is no small matter. Though one has entered the Buddha-dharma, donned the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*, and received the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts,
if one does not know the matter of one's own fundamental duty, nor knows the suffering of birth and death within the three realms, but merely remains attached to this skull,
deeming that one may preserve it for a hundred years and lingering in attachment to the dusty world— how could such a person know of the five [fires] in the ten-thousand-fathom deep pit?
The fire of desire burns the heart day and night; the thieves of the six sense organs inflict injury at every moment.

Though one possesses the name of having left home and received the precepts, one lacks the reality of benefiting oneself and others. When impermanence suddenly arrives, one passes through an entire lifetime in unawareness and unknowing.
Not only is one lifetime wasted, but it is feared that hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes will all follow from this very point.
It is all mixed up and confused. Therefore, the ancient masters said: "Hell is not yet the ultimate suffering; to lose one's human body while beneath the *kāṣāya* is the greatest suffering.
O worthy ones, a human body is difficult to obtain, the Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear, and a virtuous friend is difficult to encounter.
This assembly today is no small matter. For this reason, I do not begrudge the bitterness of my words as I urge you on. From this day forward...
Go! Each of you should give rise to the mind that transcends the world, establish the resolve for transcendence, and practice the deeds of transcendence.

As years pass and months accumulate, these practices will become second nature; naturally and gradually, you will be able to transform the three poisons into the three clusters of pure precepts, transform the six consciousnesses into the six supernormal powers, transform afflictions into bodhi, and transform ignorance into great wisdom—without depending on anything external.
This is simply the constant nature of one’s own mind. Again, it is cited that when the novice Gao visited Yaoshan, Yaoshan asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "I have come from Mount Nanyue. Yaoshan said, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to Jiangling to receive the full precepts.
Yaoshan asked, "What do you hope to gain by receiving the precepts? He replied, "I hope to escape birth and death. Yaoshan said, "There is a person who..."
"Receiving the precepts likewise cannot exempt one from birth and death. Do you understand? He replied, "If that is so, then what use are the Buddha’s precepts?
The Master said, "This śrāmaṇera still has words on his lips. That evening, as he ascended the hall, the Master called out, "Where was the śrāmaṇera who came this morning?
The Śrāmaṇera Gao stepped forward from the assembly. The Master said, "I heard that Chang’an is very noisy; have you [heard it]?"
"Do you understand? The novice Gao said, "My country is at peace. Shanshan asked, "Why do you not receive the precepts?
The novice Gao said, "Knowing such matters as these, one simply lets them be; what else would one call 'precepts'?
The Master said, "When the novice Gao first resolved to receive the precepts, he intended to escape birth and death. How fierce was his resolve! Yet when Yaoshan..."
He brought forth this faceless fellow, wishing to meet him. When the fellow arrived there, he was filled with doubt and asked, "If that is so, then what use are the Buddha's precepts?
Upon hearing Yaoshan say, "This śrāmaṇera still has his teeth hanging on his lips," he finally knew where to return.
Therefore, Yaoshan examined him again, saying, "Cháng'ān is very noisy. He immediately understood and replied, "In my kingdom, all is peaceful."
Indeed. From this point on, he no longer hangs within the sun and moon of the mundane realm; he stands alone beyond the heavens and earth of the kalpa.
His solemn and lofty wind has not been succeeded by anyone for a thousand ages. Even so, every great man has nostrils beneath his skin, and who among them lacks blood under their hide?
How could they willingly remain submerged like a land-sunk object, refusing to seek liberation? I dare ask the assembly: suppose that...
Yaoshan said: "There is one person who does not receive the precepts and yet has no birth-and-death from which to be exempted.
But ultimately, who is this? Investigate!
(This was a tea-talk.)
The Master said: "There is no need to practice Zen; there is no need to study the Buddha-dharma.
If you simply recognize these two words, 'birth and death,' the task of a lifetime of study is finished. Therefore, the Elder Boshan used to constantly instruct people to contemplate:
'Where does birth come from? Where does death go? If you truly recognize the origin of birth and the destination of death, what else remains?"
What a matter! Nevertheless, there are three things that must also be exposed: when drinking tea, you must not let it wet your tongue;
when biting fruit, you must not let it stick to your teeth; when returning to your quarters, you must not bump into the pillar.
"If there is anyone who can penetrate these three matters, tomorrow we shall prepare a separate tea ceremony to welcome them.
If you cannot penetrate them, the day is already late; you must urgently tighten your straw sandals."
The New Year’s Eve Tea Talk. The Master said: "Tonight is New Year’s Eve. In the Cloud Hall, the lamps burn brightly and fruit platters are set out in array.
Three hundred members of the assembly have gathered here to celebrate the end of the year together, partaking of Yunmen’s cakes and drinking Zhaozhou’s tea.
As we bid farewell to the old and welcome the new, we share in the joy of peace. At this very moment, all that is seen is harmony."
All was solemn and majestic, joyous and harmonious, refined and blissful. One did not know who was guest and who was host, who was self and who was other;
who was kin and who was stranger, or who was alike and who was different.

Now that the Abbot, my elder brother Jiuyou, has brought the affairs of the monastery to a successful conclusion for the year, he wishes to provide a final commentary—adding "flowers upon brocade"—and so he cannot help but cite an ancient story.
I consult with the great assembly so that everyone may know this. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"That which is within the category of sentient beings is called Buddha-nature; that which is within the category of non-sentient beings is called Dharma-nature. I venture to ask the assembly:
what is it that, being within the category of sentient beings, is called Buddha-nature, and being within the category of non-sentient beings, is called Dharma-nature?
"Nature. From where do sentient and insentient beings come? Who established Buddha-nature and Dharma-nature? Do you understand?
Having gone from the wine jar to buy village liquor, he puts on his robe again to act as the host. Take care."
Lantern Festival Tea Talk. The Master said: "The moon marks the beginning of the year, and the festival arrives at the Lantern Festival.

One contemplates the purity of this single night, as ten thousand branches of lanterns shine brilliantly. At such a time, Dīpaṃkara Buddha manifests his bodies everywhere, and Śākyamuni receives his prediction of enlightenment in every place.
He turns the Wheel of Dharma within a single speck of dust and reveals jeweled lands upon the tip of a single hair."
If you understand it, right before your eyes, clouds wrap everything while rain sprinkles the clear sky.
If you do not understand it, right before your eyes, spring opens the flowers of the iron tree. Let us set aside for now whether one understands or does not understand. But tell me:
on ground where there is neither yin nor yang, what season is it now? After a long silence, he said: "Go drink tea."

An ancient monk cited the verse by Fushan Yuan, who saw off Touzi Qing Chan Master, as a request for instruction. The Master said: "Sumeru stands in the great void (phenomena and principle do not intersect);
the sun and moon revolve in support (the partial and the correct are interwoven). The myriad peaks gradually lean upon one another (relying on others leads to error); the white snow just begins..."

To change [is to obscure the original luminosity]. The breeze from Shaolin rises through the thickets [the clouds of delusion are blown away]; the bamboo curtain at Caoxi rolls back [the eyes are opened wide]. Does the golden phoenix perch in the dragon’s nest? [Do you see him?
How could the imperial moss be crushed by a carriage wheel? [There is no path where one can travel. He spoke again:

"If you understand that the golden phoenix perches in the dragon’s nest, you will immediately understand that Mount Sumeru stands within the great void. This is the fundamental, transcendent realm; it is not a matter of intellectual knowledge."
To reach this point, one must first attain wondrous enlightenment; everything in between is merely talk according to the occasion. Look at the commentary below.
It quotes the *Treasure Mirror Samādhi* (Pao-ching san-mei), which says: "At midnight it is perfectly bright; when daybreak comes, it is not revealed. What is meant by "perfectly bright"?
A "bottomless" phrase. [The Master] provides his own substitute saying: "The jade hare runs clutching the sun; the golden crow flies clutching the moon.
He then cites a verse by the late Master Shouchang shown to Master Boshan: "When empty presses against empty, the merit is great;
When existence presses against existence, the virtue is still slight. To slander Kāśyapa’s natural state of peace— Where one gains the advantage, one loses it."
The Master said: "Daopai, mimicking my style, has also composed a verse: A stone woman applies makeup before a wooden mirror;
An illusory person grasps a brush to write upon empty space. Celestial writing is not a character of the human world; How could true form be made dense by rouge and powder?"
A monk once finished building a stupa for Shushan’s longevity and asked him about it. Shushan said, "How much money did you give to the craftsmen?
The monk replied, "Everything was left to the Master. Shushan said, "Did you give three coins to the craftsmen? Or two coins? Or one coin?
If you can answer this, I will let you build a stupa for me yourself. The monk— [remained silent].
[The monk] remained silent. The Master said, "Master Ren holds the hook, using an ox as bait. Later, the monk related this to Master Xian of Daling Hermitage.
Xian asked, "Has anyone been able to say it? The monk replied, "No one has been able to say it yet. Xian said, "When you return, tell Shushan:
'If you give three coins to the craftsman, the Master will certainly not receive a stupa in this life.'"
"If you give two coins to the craftsman, we shall produce one hand together; if you give only one coin to the craftsman, it will cause his eyebrows and hair to fall out.
The Master said, "A single hook catches twelve giant tortoises across the mountains. The monk returned and reported exactly as he had been instructed.

Shan Juyi, observing the majestic demeanor of Daling as he prostrated and sighed, said, "I thought there was no one here, yet Great Ridge has an ancient Buddha whose light shoots forth and reaches this place.
Although it is so, it is still like a lotus blooming in the twelfth month.

Hearing these words from behind the ridge, [Daling] said, "For me to speak in such a way is already like a tortoise’s hair growing three feet long. The Master said, "If not for those subsequent words..."
"Both are blind men," he said. Then he cited Master Dahuì:
"What Heaven mandates is called nature; this is the Pure Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Following one's nature is called the Way;

this is the Perfectly Full Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Cultivating the Way is called teaching; this is the thousands of billions of Transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). The Master said, "Sublime!"

The old man Xǐ was accustomed to seizing such opportunities; at the slightest opening of the mouth, he would pierce the nostrils of Śākyamuni and Zhòngní, dragging them here and there with great ease.
Nevertheless, Upādhyāya Pèi is not like this. He takes up his staff and says:
"There is only this wooden *zhílù*. When it stands upright, let Śākyamuni’s be returned to Śākyamuni, and Zhòngní’s to Zhòngní."
The bottom belongs to Zhongni; the wondrous joy belongs to Miaoxi. Transversely!
The life and nature of Śākyamuni, Zhongni, and Miaoxi are all here, shattered into a hundred fragments. At this very moment, when neither horizontal nor vertical—how do you speak a single phrase?
Listen to this verse: The great void is vast and empty; who would set up fences there? The blue sea is wide and deep...
Vast and expansive—who built these banks and embankments? Without cause, they are propped up and then toppled. It makes one laugh to see this mountain monk with his staff of cane.
This staff of cane—no one knows it. Transcending spring and autumn, what could it possibly do? For years it has leaned against the corner of the wall.
"Let him draw his own branches in secret.

*Pah!* [The Master] raised the case where Jingqing asked Caoshan: "When the principle of ultimate vacuity has no body, what then? Caoshan said, "It is too noble. Jingqing asked, "The principle is thus;
but as for the phenomenon, what is it? Caoshan said, "One must recognize it on another peak. The Master said, "One must recognize it on another peak."
[Zhao]qing said, "It is seen as it is, according to principle and according to fact. The Master said, "Seeing an egg and seeking the rooster—is that not too early?
[Zhao]qing said, "One may deceive Cao Shan alone, but what about the eyes of the thousand sages? The Master said, "It is not that Cao Shan would have let this pass.
[Zhao]qing said, "If there were no eyes of the thousand sages, how could one discern that it is not so? The Master said, "Indeed."
Dongshan said, "Forcefully act as the sovereign. Dongshan replied, "The official does not permit even a needle, yet private traffic passes through carts and horses.
The Master said, "Only when you speak in this way will the discourse finally become complete. He further remarked, "Regarding this koan, although there have been many critiques since antiquity..."
Those who have grasped the essential meaning are very few. Today, braving ridicule, I shall provide a commentary from the beginning.

Nevertheless, as for Jingqing’s saying, “In accordance with principle, in accordance with phenomena”—if this single turn of phrase were under the gate of another school, one might walk away freely and at ease;
yet having arrived here at the gate of Caodong, it is truly a journey of thousands of miles. Therefore, Zhenru...
It is said: Although Jingqing’s jade is naturally flawless, alas, it has not yet been fashioned by a skilled hand and remains a discarded vessel.
But tell me, where does the error lie? The verse says: Within this, there is originally no rank or position; The collateral path traverses the orthodox, the deviant, and the perfect.
To go directly toward that "other side" according to phenomena and principle— Is it any different from looking up and spitting at the blue sky?
The Buddha-work is profoundly examined:
the Zen practitioner lowers his head and does not see the earth; he looks up and does not see the sky. If you wish to recognize the adamantine body, simply look before the skull.
"The skull is here; where is the vajra-body? Does the Venerable Xuankao still know this?

If you do know it, then this very thing was originally unborn in the past and is likewise unextinguished now. If you have not yet realized this, [the Master] brandishes a torch, draws a circle, and says:
'In these towering flames reaching to the heavens, one must turn back; look at that single snowflake in the red furnace. Then he struck.
The fire is lit.
Kejun, head of the firewood, takes a torch and draws a circle in the air, saying: "Today we perform the cremation for Kejun, the head of the firewood. Tell me, how does this compare to the past?"
As for Dayu丹霞 burning the wooden Buddha—were they the same or different? [Dayu] threw down a torch and said: "After the fire, a single stalk of thatch.
Cheng’an上座 took the torch and drew a circle in the air, saying: "It is like a great mass of fire; fierce flames break out simultaneously, yet each does not..."
"Mutual understanding. All dharmas are also like this. Again, he drew a circle and said, "Just so, just so.
He then cast down a torch and said, "The Venerable Cheng’an should simply let out his breath right here."
"Xinti, you who are wary of the fire of the human heart;
Elder Xinti, you left home in your prime with a keen resolve to enter the Way. In speech and silence you were not casual, and in movement and stillness you never strayed from the proper path;
you were truly one of constant virtue within the monastic community. Yet, alas, your life was too short; you passed away at the young age of twenty-nine."
In his final year, he was afflicted by illness and suddenly passed away; how can one bear such grief and regret! Nevertheless, you have spoken these words:
"I have already understood this matter; seeing the emptiness of the aggregates, what more is there to say? Birth and death, longevity and early demise, are like flowers in the sky.
Indeed, there is no place to find arising or ceasing. This morning, I escort you into that very midst. Furthermore, there is one more thing: [The text ends here.]
The Final Instruction. But tell me, what is this final instruction? He raises a torch and says, "Do you understand? The numinous light pierces through the vast void;
for thousands and tens of thousands of miles, it is but a single bar of iron. With a shout, he extinguishes the fire.
"The virtue of Qian is fire:
Yuan, Li, Heng, and Zhen; this is the virtue of Qian. It begins with the One Qi (One Breath). But tell me, what does this One Qi itself begin from?
Holding up a torch, he said: "Do you understand? 'I see the Lamp-Bright Buddha; his original radiance is such as this. He then set it down.
Fire. Sending off Great Master Qiu Cun into his stupa:
snow covers the ten thousand peaks and myriad mountains; solitary peaks stand far apart, their rugged faces exposed. At midnight, the wooden man lightly extends [his hand].
With his hands, he shattered Yunmen’s "Single-Word Barrier. I respectfully venerate the Great Master Qicun, a senior elder of the precept platform and a veteran of the Dharma community.
He disciplines himself with austere purity, possessing the integrity of a cold pine amidst the snow; he receives others with compassionate harmony, like a midday lotus radiating fragrance.

Ancient in countenance and ancient in heart, his conduct and withdrawal are grounded in principle. His realization is authentic and his practice is genuine; his vision and feet do not err. Having cast aside...
Once the leather bag has been scorched by the fierce fire and the śarīra have been recovered after a hundred refinements, they may finally be stored forever within a seamless stūpa.
From this point on, neither cold nor heat shall shift them, and neither the mundane nor the sagely shall recognize them.

At such a time, when heaven and earth are cut off and one alone transcends the realm beyond, how do you speak the single phrase? "When spring ends in the Ten Continents, the flowers wither; atop the shadowless tree..."
The sun shines brightly.
It has been several autumns since the Venerable Dashou entered the stupa and hung his staff at Nanzen-ji;
single-mindedly maintaining one thought, he severed all seeking. With his causes fulfilled and his fruits perfected, he returns to the West.
Go! Only upon reaching this point is it called the Great Rest. Nevertheless, even so, how can one say that this "something" still remains?
Today, it is gathered back into the stūpa; throughout the mundane and supramundane worlds, there is no obstruction.
Seeing off my inner friend Rou Chan into the stupa—how were our shared practices in days of old?
Before the lamp and beneath the moon, we polished one another; now upon the White Cloud Peak we meet again, once more seeing you off to the *stūpa*.
As for the phrase "settling one's home and finding joy in one’s work," how would you speak of it?
Casting down the sacred remains, he said: "The light of the black pearl blazes forth; the shadow of the moon and cassia sways.
He thus escorted the Dharma-friend Chan Master Fazhen into the stupa.

As for the Venerable Fazhen, throughout his life he harbored great ambitions; he discussed the profound and expounded the wondrous, manipulating the spiritual mechanisms and seeking out true companions.
The Master and his disciples poured forth their spirit and intent; now that the work of this single fire is accomplished, they cannot help but return to this place.
But tell me, after returning to this place, what then? "The clear pool does not permit the azure dragon to coil; Heaven and earth are at his disposal for play."
Sending off my Zen friend Zhuo-sheng into the stupa:
Neither non-arising nor arising; standing tall and solitary. Who can receive him? The stone woman opens her door at night.
Now tell me, how does one enter this gate? Within the skull, the eyes are open; black as the sun, yet bright as lacquer.
[This concludes] the enshrinement of the remains of Master Songzhong in the stupa.
Venerable Elders, before arriving here, host and guest were distinct and self and object were separate.
Now that we have arrived here, object and self are fused and host and guest are one. The fences having been removed, there is a vast and great equilibrium.
Tell me, what place is this? Do you understand? Beneath the shadowless tree, they share the same boat; driven by the wind to the shore, no one recognizes them.

As we escort the spirit-bones of our various parents into the Baoqin Pagoda, each person has had a father and each person has had a mother; yet today they all gather here, and only then do we realize there is neither "that" nor "this."
Although it is thus, let us not speak of the destruction of the seal of the Sahā world. How is it when a single phrase of the Pure Land text is formed?
A wooden man sings on the mountain ridges; a stone woman dances by the stream.
The verse shows that they are not different:

the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand forms are fundamentally no different from the practitioner of dhyāna. To lengthen the ducks' legs or shorten the cranes' is but a vain labor of the spirit. One need only be able to maintain a single thought free from self-interest.
Depart! Beyond the kalpas, the scenery is freshly cut and new.
To the Zen practitioner Tanshui, I show that the *utpala* flower marks a sublime destiny;
it blooms uniquely from within the fire, its numinous roots coil beyond the kalpas, and its fruit of the Way will ripen for the future.
Auspicious vapors pervade the universe; pure qi extends throughout the nine realms. The spring season seems entirely untouched by human effort, yet it vainly requires cultivation and nurturing.
Showing the dwelling from which Chan practitioners emerge:
the three realms offer no peace, like a house on fire. This single gate leading far beyond the ordinary—on the white ox-cart, one rides with body erect.
Amidst the land of venomous insects, do not taste the water. Who needs to rely on external power to topple the illusory city? Ascend directly to the precious destination alone.
Transcending the mundane: a man of resolve should be thus. Do not wait until you stand at the crossroads to lose the sheep.
Truly, this illusory body of the four elements will soon perish; in an instant, dream-like thoughts turn into delusion. A lifetime spent in restless toil and haste.
Depart! Who can claim this fleeting fame?
If one can overturn the conventional molds of this Sahā world, Only then may one dwell within the lotus chambers of Sukhāvatī. When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is naturally attained.
Purity. An auspicious sign appeared from within the fire as a lotus flower.
Once, while ill, he personally decocted medicine; composing a verse on the mutual treatment of illness and medicine to admonish himself:
"A skull decocts medicine to heal a skull. Which skull will ever reach the end of healing? If one recognizes that body and mind are fundamentally non-existent..."
Sickness: a thousand kinds of medicines are all forbidden at once.
Behold the entire earth—nothing is not sickness; behold the entire earth—nothing is not medicine. Medicine and sickness treating one another is but a single occasion;
how could that matter ever have been lightly moved?
Vimalakīrti lay ill in Vaiśālī; within the Gate of Non-duality, he tested the masters of the Way. A single silence was like thunder, awakening the hibernating insects;
yet even so, it remains but sand in the eye.

The World-Honored One appeared in the world as the King of Physicians; for over forty years he preached medicinal prescriptions, yet in the end he could not heal himself, and until now he lies prostrate in the Hall of Nirvana.
The Supplement to the Amitābha Sūtra, using verses from the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, describes the practice of profound *prajñā*:

"When practicing profound *prajñā-pāramitā*, one clearly perceives that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are empty and thus transcends suffering and calamity. Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is precisely form.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Śāriputra, wishing to know the characteristics of the emptiness of phenomena, realizes birth-and-death, defilement, and purity.

There is none. Therefore, within emptiness, the aggregates and elements do not exist; the truths, conditions, and perfections likewise cannot be apprehended. Because there is nothing to be apprehended, one attains bodhi.
This is the unsurpassed power of the divine wisdom of prajñā.
Enjoying the Moon on Mid-Autumn (Two Poems) Who has hung this precious mirror in the vast sky?

A single expanse of luminous clarity falls before my eyes. Its radiance flows across the earth, solitary and far-reaching; Its reflection in a thousand rivers is harmonious and bright. The world grinds it down through ages, yet its light does not diminish; Hanshan and Shide discuss its intent and spirit. Who has hung this precious mirror in the vast sky?

A single expanse of luminous clarity falls before my eyes. Its radiance flows across the earth, solitary and far-reaching; Its reflection in a thousand rivers is harmonious and bright. The world grinds it down through ages, yet its light does not diminish; Hanshan and Shide discuss its intent and spirit.
Spontaneous realization. A gathering of monks watches as pure inspiration arises; one knows not how many share this same insight. When the moon reaches mid-autumn, it is doubly magnificent:
ten times pure and full, it emerges from the eastern peaks. Its reflection scatters across the clear river like a thousand pearls;

its solitary brilliance in the azure sky is a single sphere of jade. Amidst the trees, the whistling wind is even more serene; the flowers in the courtyard are intoxicated by the dew, their colors vibrant.

It is especially cold; I joyfully compose fine verses to celebrate this auspicious season. As the sun turns westward like a skipping ball, I present these words to Pan Shanzǐ, a man of talent who was recommended as a filial and incorruptible official (*xiàolián*).

Having entered the academy at the age of childhood, he achieved renown immediately upon reaching adulthood. Filiality and integrity are innate to his nature, and his literary compositions adhere to the established models.
The dragon slumbers in the abyss, yet may leap; the leopard hides in the mist, awaiting the dawn. Behold the spring thunder burst forth; it seizes the clouds and soars far away. I see you, Mr.
Pan Shige, the retired father of Shanzi, the Licentiate, who has long lain within his gate at Heng, finding joy in Heaven.
Now that your worthy son has passed the imperial examination, you must spur him on further. When one attains glory and success, all else becomes trivial.

Matters of loyalty and filial piety are the legacy passed down through generations; father and son ride side by side as the instructions of the household are earnestly applied. When sovereign and minister meet, the imperial strategy is proclaimed;
after hearing the names called from the steps, one may take staff and sandals to climb the mountain and inquire of the Zen masters.
The ancestral stupa of Caoshan was secretly opened by a monk, who discovered that the entire body remained, with the bones and stone intact.
The skull was as large as a peck-measure (*dou*), the teeth were white as jade, and his height was approximately nine feet.
Startled, they resealed the tomb. When Master Zhuhong of Shouchang heard of this matter, he went to open the crypt and examine it; indeed, it was exactly as reported.
The Biography continues: He then plotted to rebuild the stupa and composed a verse to record the event, using the rhyme of Master Lang:
"A drunken man from under Dongshan’s gate; he hides his body in the place of no change. One day he emerges to give it to others."
Look! Only then will you know that my Way has long remained ever-new. Everywhere, the descendants are all nourished by the Dharma-milk.
Shouchang is nearby and serves as the master; the seamless stupa stands once more majestic. Its reflection falls upon Xiangtan—who can recommend it?
Eight lay practitioners from Shouning requested a verse from Bangcai.
Where does this state of affairs come from? It is vividly present, like a mirror upon its stand; meeting conditions, it manifests, yet remains detached from the mind.
The mind fundamentally possesses radiance that pervades the nine realms.
Just as the transformations of dragons and spirits are unfathomable, this spiritual mind is even more difficult to conceive; when its great function manifests, it leaves no trace.
Thus, why need one needlessly give rise to further doubt?
Mounting the wondrous Dharma-vehicle of the White Ox, one grasps the reins and flies straight home; there is no need to seek escape from the burning house.
Depart! The message within this is like a lotus flower.

The fundamental nature of the celestial transformation is originally without words; through silent cultivation, it is brought to fruition. The four seasons and ten thousand things unfold spontaneously; one need only be able to personally realize this wordlessness.
The profound meaning is this: the child created by the powers of transformation is my own birth;
the pervasive hand and eye throughout the body is Avalokiteśvara.
Universally responding to the human world, his vow-power is deep; with a single thought of taking refuge, his entire being is revealed.
Manifest: the precious jewel is in the palm; there is no need to seek it.
The sensitive mind-king is itself subtle and wondrous like an empty valley; the call and response are simultaneous, never erring. Thus one recognizes the true nature of one's own mind.
The abode of the great chiliocosm is but a single bubble upon a flower.
How warm was Confucius in days of yore, most gentle and reverent; he revitalized this culture as a patriarch for a hundred generations. Where fish leap and kites soar, there is no distinction.
The Dharma: Śākyamuni’s nostrils share a common wind.

As for Yan Yuan’s joy—how could his ultimate state of bliss have lain merely in dwelling within a humble alley of coarse mats and gourds? If you wish to recognize this intimate reality, look no further.
[This is] the dwelling place. Not departing from it all day long, he remains as if a simpleton.
To Elder Layman Wang Shoufeng on his sixtieth birthday:
Lord Wang is a fellow student of mine. He has devoted himself to this Way for many years. This is the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month.

On the occasion of the Master’s sixtieth birthday, his worthy sons and excellent grandsons gathered in great numbers before him. They vied with one another in painting pine trees and rocks as a means of congratulation.
The Master laughed and said, "As for these trivial pine trees and rocks, you may find them sufficient for yourselves; however, the cultivation of such aesthetic sentiments is not my concern."
He then sent a letter inquiring of me regarding matters prior to the birth of one's parents. Elder Yi had attained profound realization in this regard;
he intended to perpetuate it for eternity and merely sought to express it through my words.

As for someone like myself, insignificant as a mere pine or rock, how could I possibly compare my own measure to his? Knowing that the Elder’s intent lay therein, I have idly taken up the brush to write.
The pines grow ever green and the stones grow ever firm; I raise this to wish you long life, yet you, O Venerable One, say "not so.

You have sent a letter to question me regarding that which exists prior to birth—how can the news from within this state be transmitted? In the single silence of Vaiśālī, the true teaching was revealed; the Gate of Non-duality opened to receive those with the karmic affinity.

Only you, Venerable One, possess wondrous realization prior to the movement of the occasion; without leaving the realm of the five aggregates, you are liberated from the bonds of delusion. A clay ox emerges from the sea.

Waves splash the heavens; they plow through the three thousand and the great chiliocosm. Let the *xiányuán* sexagenary cycle shift as it may; floating light and illusory shadows are perfected within a dream.
Where in empty space can one find center or periphery? Encompassing heaven and wrapping the earth, it continues on and on of its own accord.
For you, old man, I have written out this complete countenance; I know from afar that a single smile will resound throughout the mundane world.

Seeing off Zen Practitioner Zhizang as he returns to Shouchang, I am reminded of that old man with his straw raincoat and bamboo hat of yore. Plowing deep and sowing shallow, he had no claim to merit.
As you return, should anyone ask about the road to the far reaches of the night, tell them the affairs in the fields are in full bloom.
Seeing off Zen practitioner Hengzhen as he returns to Shouchang:
To stand where one is is itself the truth; there is no need for external support. When the heels touch the ground, one knows the sound for oneself.
Beneath the bridge at Shouchang, the waters of the Gan River flow vast and wide toward the east, without beginning or end.
Exhort your fellow practitioners to awaken to your own mind and cultivate your own truth; do not vainly grasp at worldly sentiments and seek elsewhere.

Limited time and light easily pass away; when will this boundless cycle of birth and death ever cease? Momentary conceptualizations are like the flickering of a lamp’s flame—this entire body is but one.
Skull: Throughout the twelve hours of the day, you must recognize the master; do not allow a fleeting thought to arise and mistake it for a floating bubble.

The Great Way that came from the West points directly; when the mind falls into conceptualization, there are myriad deviations. To see and understand down to the subtlest detail is purely consciousness;

when the sharp edge of the spiritual pivot transcends categories, it is altogether not Chan. To investigate and exhaust the ultimate principle is the rule for awakening; to tread the profound path is to realize.
Thus it is complete. Do not study those of the present day who are like mouth-drums; their entanglements will bind them until the year of the donkey.

Scribe: Taijing. Recorded is the Verse on the Five Ranks of Dongshan.
The partial within the absolute: since the roof was broken, the blue sky is revealed; the obscurity of kalpas is suddenly clarified. Myriad dharmas are blended as one within a silver bowl;
the single truth is uniquely exposed before the bright moon. The mountain of form possesses jewels—when have they ever been hidden? When the great earth is free of dust, [the light shines forth].
Abandon them. If principle and measure are not yet resolved, they will form thorns of dogmatic views; like lingering clouds and mist, they remain entangled.

Within the profound palace of "correctness within partiality," silently embody non-action (*wuwei*). You must be taught to follow this in obedience without ever departing from it for a moment. When not a single thought arises, one merges with the dark, fundamental source.
Sublime! The slightest movement falls into the present moment. Bare and naked before the sound, one diligently bears the burden; empty and void within the Dharma, one reverently maintains it.
Before the great function has even turned, the child is born; yet as before, one enters and exits, traversing the realms of transcendence and subtlety.
Coming from the very center, one traverses the streams and mountains to reach that place; with pure light filling the eyes, one is not permitted to sleep.

As the single hue gradually fades on the moon atop the terrace, the numinous mechanism suddenly manifests as a lotus within the fire. Having cast off the jeweled crown, how could there be any lingering attachment? Walking along the bird-path, the steps proceed.
From the profound mystery: in its application, it simply enables one to pass through without transgression; following the teaching, one treads upon level ground and walks across the blue sky.

Simultaneously reaching the ultimate, he pulls open the golden lock to reveal his entire body. His wondrous function, sweeping and expansive, is utterly beyond compare. He rides a wooden horse backward as it soars through the azure heavens.

The Master’s lineage lamp is a rhinoceros torch; his Dharma-sea is a dragon pearl. Having resolved upon the bodhicitta in past kalpas, his compassion is inherently complete.

The sound of a coughing sneeze extinguishes the traces of the jeweled transformation-city. From this point on, the great white ox roams freely east and west;
at the waters of Caoxi, one encounters the source from every direction. A pure gold shop is opened amidst the four mountains, its price set as high as the vast heavens;
the New Feng melody is sung through the five ranks, its spontaneous song resonating with layered reflections. Thus, one skillfully enters the Treasure Mirror Samādhi.
The profound mechanism is vast and open. He is accustomed to threading the noseless golden needle;

he employs ordinary means to snatch away food and drive the plow, yet applies extraordinary hammers and tongs to beat the bones and extract the marrow. Upon the towering peaks, the waves of Dharma are vast and boundless;

along the path that pierces the heavens, the sacred trees stand in dense shade. A hundred birds nest together, and the four seas meet as one. Now that this period of seeking alms has concluded, what hindrance could there be?
Withdrawing from the clamor, the sun of wisdom has sunk; let it be as it may for this one to efface their traces. Since idle fame has been cast aside, it cannot be sought within the three realms.

The skull is suddenly dried up, severing all across the ten directions. We, the undersigned, have committed ourselves to the furnace and bellows, yet we regret our own dullness and difficulty in being refined.

Having served as members of the monastic community, we feel shame for our negligence and failure in duty. Now that we encounter these calamities at the Crane Forest (Kāśyapa’s Grove), we harbor deep resentment.

In the sorrow of losing my protector, I constantly cherish the sound of the lion’s roar; my long-standing lament for the parting at the crossroads is ever stirred. The mountain winds and ocean moon seem to manifest their presence before me;
the dew on the grass and the moisture of the flowers—how can they bear my shedding of tears? I respectfully present this final offering to extend my sincerity in mourning the deceased.

My wailing fails to form coherent sounds, and my words frequently lose their order. Alas! How tragic! I humbly pray that you will graciously accept this offering. *Fuwēi shàngxiǎng.* (I humbly pray that you will graciously accept this offering.)
The Inscription for the Stupa of the Great Zen Master Yongjue Xian of Gushan: He was a successor of the Venerable Shouchang Wuming.
It is recorded that he belonged to the thirty-second generation of the Caodong lineage. His native place was Jianyang; his surname was Cai. He was born during the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty.
On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the year of Wuyin (1638), at the hour of Si, he who had studied Confucianism since childhood and harbored great ambitions composed a poem that said:
"In virtue and conduct, I take Yan Hui and Min Ziqian as my teachers; in literature, I follow Youzi and Xiahou. As for the other two or three disciples, I have no desire to rank beneath them.
At the age of twenty, he was enrolled as a student in the local school (*xiang*). However, by nature he was serene and aloof, finding no pleasure in the worldly clamor. At twenty-five—
While studying at a mountain temple, he heard a monk reciting the Lotus Sūtra: “At that time, I manifested for them a body of pure radiance.

Suddenly, he was overcome with such joy that he could not contain himself. He sighed deeply and exclaimed, “Outside the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, there truly exists this other great matter!

From then on, he devoted himself to the vehicles of the Buddhist teachings, mastering both the sūtras and the śāstras. When he looked back upon the secular classics, they no longer seemed worth his attention.
Like the ocean compared to a cow’s footprint, he considered himself to have attained realization.

After some time, when the Venerable Wuming Shouchang began teaching the Dharma at Dongyan in Yiyang, [Zhaozhou] heard his proclamations and was utterly bewildered, losing all sense of self-assurance. He sighed, saying, "How can a painted cake ever satisfy hunger?
Thereupon, he completely abandoned what he had previously studied and followed Shouchang to practice Zen. One day, he heard a monk cite the story of the killing of the cat.
Suddenly, he attained realization. He composed a verse and presented it to Chang. Chang said, "This matter cannot be grasped through a single trigger or a single circumstance.
Although one may pass directly through even a hundred enclosures and a thousand layers with hands hanging down, one must still meet the right person before it is truly achieved. As the saying goes:
'Not knowing that one is already atop the blue clouds, yet further casting one's body into the multitude of storehouses'—this is the eye of one who studies the Way. The Master [then understood].

Withdrawing, he applied himself to his investigation with even greater vigor. Upon reaching the age of forty, he finally tore apart his scholar’s robes, abandoned his wife and children, and followed Shouchang to shave his head.
Whenever anyone later came to question him, Shouchang would simply say, "I am not as good as you. One day, while returning from the fields, Shouchang encountered the Master;
the Master went forward to ask, "What is the pure, luminous body? Shouchang stood up straight and tall.

The Master stepped forward and said, "Is there anything else besides this? Chang immediately walked away. At that moment, the Master suddenly felt a sense of liberation, as if a heavy burden had been lifted from his shoulders.
He followed him into the abbot’s quarters; as he prostrated and rose to communicate what he had attained, Chang abruptly seized his staff and struck him three times, saying:
"In the future, you must not be careless. He then showed him a verse, saying: "Each time one penetrates through, it becomes deeper;

from of old, Buddhas and Patriarchs have not permitted others [to know]. Even if one were to leap onto the back of the Golden-Haired Lion, they would still cause one to turn over for oneself beneath the staff.
The Master remained in doubt, asking, "Why must one further turn over beneath the staff? After Chang passed away, he relied upon his fellow disciple Bo...
Master Shanwu of Chan Temple remained for three years, during which time he received full ordination. Subsequently, he took leave to return to Mount Min to dwell there.
While crossing the Jian River by boat, he heard a monk chanting the Lotus Sūtra: “At that time, they all coughed and snapped their fingers together;
these two sounds reached throughout the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions. At this, he attained a vast and sudden awakening, thoroughly penetrating the essential function of Shouchang.
A verse says: The golden rooster pecks through the azure lapis lazuli; Ten thousand cessations and a thousand restings are known only to oneself.
Reclining peacefully on a single sail under a clear sky, On the mountain ahead, the rain-birds no longer cry. This was in the ninth month of autumn in the *guihai* year of the Tianqi era.
The Master was forty-six years of age. Having attained the Way, he lived in seclusion in accordance with conditions.
He first resided at the Jinxian Hermitage in Oning for three years, and subsequently moved to Mount Heshan by Dongxi in Jian’an for eight years.
There, he lived by tending fires and farming with a knife, completely cutting off contact with the world. At the age of fifty-six, he went to visit the Great Master Wengu at Baoshan. One—

The following year, he accepted an invitation to Mount Gu; yet, he continued to reside as a hermitage master (*amaju*).

Two years later, he opened the Dharma at Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou, while Huidao began to propagate the incense of his realization, which had been brought forth by the Elder Wuming. The Master once said: "Chan is fundamentally from Shouchang; the precepts are fundamentally..."
"Zhenji (True Tranquility) cannot be falsely attributed [to another]. Subsequently, he established the Dharma at Zhenji in Hangzhou and invited [the master] to Baoshan.
Later, he returned to Gushan, where he reconstructed the monastic buildings and extensively propagated the school’s teachings. All within the realm revered him as an "Ancient Buddha.
On the first day of the ninth month in the Dingyou year of the Qing Shunzhi era, he manifested a slight ailment. On the seventh day of the tenth month, at midnight..."
At that time, he spoke a verse and addressed the assembly; then, sitting upright, he passed away. He was eighty years of age and had been ordained for forty-one years.

On the twenty-first day of the first month of the following year, at the hour of the horse (noon), his entire body was enshrined in a stupa in the western fields of the monastery, in accordance with his final instructions.
His recorded teachings from three assemblies and his various writings total twenty works, comprising over eighty fascicles; all of these were widely circulated.
In this world,

the inscription for the opening of the reliquary chamber was prepared on the auspicious day of the first *shen* hour on the twenty-first day of the first month in the fifteenth year of the Shunzhi era. By the Dharma-heir disciple:
Dao Pai, leading the assembly of disciples from the various mountains, reverently presents this offering of incense from the Hall of Fragrant Accumulations.
We solemnly announce before the sacred reliquary of our late Master, the Great Monk Master Yong of Gushan, saying: Ah, our late Elder Master!

The vast void is your coffin, and your entire being is already enshrined therein. Yet with every step upon the green mountains, your great function is now flourishing; you have not departed from Bodhi.

He ascended to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations by stepping upon the arena; following the ancient tracks of Vairocana, he did not leave the Hall of the Holy Arrow but returned to the Seamless Stūpa.

Following the established model of the Stone Drum, he rode a wooden horse through the void and pursued a jade elephant beyond the kalpas. With a wind of purity blowing coolly, his transformation of the Way spread far and wide;
the Buddhas of the ten directions praised him beyond measure, and the disciples of the fourfold assembly gazed up at him with reverence.
[Portion]. Heh! May all together ascend the path to the eternal night and turn the True Dharma Wheel of our Master. May you enjoy this offering.
The Inscription for the Enshrinement of the Stupa:

Dao Pai, leading the assembly of disciples from the various mountains, respectfully presents this offering of food from the Fragrant Accumulation Hall.
He solemnly proclaims before the stupa of his late Master, the Venerable Abbot Yong of Shiguang Temple, who entered nirvana in the Hall of Mount Gu: "Alas!
Our late Master was the true successor of Shouchang and the principal master of Shiguang. He fully resolved the public case of his youth and caused the Buddhist monastery to be restored."
He has shaken up the collapsing lineage of Caodong; his Dharma banner stands tall, its great fame resounding through the universe.

Both those who know him and those who do not look up to his virtuous influence. His transformative rain falls across mountains and rivers; both sentient and insentient beings alike partake of the milk of the Dharma.

Now that cause is perfected and fruit is fulfilled, and the water reaches the channel, he has cast open the gate of Great Quiescent Samādhi and entered it with his whole being, raising high the [Dharma] tree.
The form of this seamless stupa shall be gazed upon for ten thousand ages. It stands as lofty and towering as Mount Li, surging together with the sacred source.
At such a time, one sits firmly, severing the heads of the Reward and Transformation Buddhas, and pierces open the eyes of humanity and the heavens.
The sound of the dharma is vibrantly heard in the pine winds and the birdsong; the realm of quiescent light is expansively perceived in the sea moon, mountain clouds, and vast sky. The Great Void...

It may perish, yet the matter remains unimpeded; though the kalpa-fire blazes fiercely, this does not decay. Protected by a hundred spirits and taken as refuge by the myriad phenomena—may you enjoy this offering.

through this, one knows that there is no such father without such a son. Alas! The spiritual resonance between father and son was like a needle meeting its eye-pin;
their magnificent virtue and great achievement are beyond all comparison. I, too, am but a "qilin-xun" (a hollow imitation) of the Dong family.
